name: AgentForge
summary: Turns a plain-English description into a schema-validated agent specification, then runs it through a LangGraph plan → act → observe → reflect loop against real tools over MCP — with per-project isolation for chats, agents, knowledge bases, and memory.
outcome: agents run against real tools over MCP, not mocked

detail.problem: Building an agent today usually means hand-writing a spec, wiring tool integrations by hand, and hoping the LLM's stated capabilities actually match what it can do. AgentForge collapses that into one flow: describe the agent in a sentence, get a JSON Schema-validated spec back, and catch capability mismatches before anything runs — via a semantic checker that flags cases where the spec claims a capability it doesn't actually need.
architectureNotes: Meta-agent pipeline: prompt → local LLM (Ollama) → structured Agent Spec → schema validation with retry-on-malformed-output → semantic capability check.
Unresolved details (a missing URL, a missing recipient) surface as inline, answerable fields rather than a dead-end error list.
Execution runs through a LangGraph plan → act → observe → reflect loop, calling real tools over MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool servers.
Every layer — MCP tool servers, the FastAPI control plane, the Next.js frontend, Postgres, Redis, and Ollama — runs as an independently deployable process wired together over HTTP.
Projects are isolated containers: each has its own chats, agents, Chroma-backed knowledge base, and persistent cross-run agent memory.
highlights: Semantic checker catches spec/capability mismatches an LLM would otherwise silently hallucinate past.
Agents can be edited and re-saved as new versions, or exported as a standalone, self-contained Docker bundle.
Full step-by-step run traces are persisted alongside a human-readable summary of what a run actually produced.

name: VelocityLB
summary: A Layer-7 load balancer built from scratch in Go, implementing four routing strategies — round-robin, least-connections, Power of Two Choices, and EWMA latency-aware routing — with active/passive health checking, AIMD concurrency limiting, and an empirical benchmark harness.

detail.problem: One backend was given 500ms of artificial latency while two others stayed healthy. Round-robin — which routes purely by turn-taking with no awareness of backend state — kept sending it a full third of all traffic regardless, dragging p99 to 503ms. Every adaptive strategy kept p99 under 100ms instead: least-connections at 66ms, P2C at 87ms, EWMA at 98ms.
architectureNotes: cmd/lb runs the load balancer; cmd/mockbackend is a configurable test backend (artificial delay, failure rate); cmd/loadgen is a concurrent load generator producing per-request CSV output.
internal/backend tracks atomic connection counts, EWMA latency, and an AIMD concurrency limiter per backend; internal/proxy implements the Strategy interface behind all four routing algorithms.
A Server-Sent-Events layer (internal/broadcast) drives a live traffic-visualization dashboard.
Python analysis scripts compute p50/p95/p99 and generate comparison charts from the benchmark CSVs; a Docker Compose stack runs Prometheus + Grafana for live observability.
highlights: P2C (Power of Two Choices) samples 2 of N backends and routes to whichever has fewer active connections — the same technique used internally by Envoy and HAProxy.
EWMA routing tracks a rolling average response time per backend and combines it with P2C-style sampling — the same approach as Envoy's PeakEWMA balancer.
The full benchmark sweep (3 scenarios × 4 strategies) and chart generation is scripted end-to-end, not run and recorded by hand.

name: Autonomous Site Reliability Engine
summary: A multi-agent system that watches a Kubernetes cluster, diagnoses real incidents using RAG grounded in a curated knowledge base of known failure modes, and generates and verifies remediation commands — closing the loop without a human in it.

detail.problem: Most self-healing setups either script a fixed set of remediations or hand root-cause analysis entirely to an LLM with no grounding — meaning it can confidently generate a plausible-sounding fix for the wrong problem. This project splits the work across dedicated agents and grounds diagnosis in a real knowledge base of Kubernetes failure modes rather than raw LLM guesswork.
architectureNotes: A monitor/watchdog process continuously observes cluster state and hands off detected anomalies.

A diagnostic agent performs RAG (agents/diagnostic/rag.py) over a curated knowledge base of Kubernetes issues (knowledge/k8s_issues.txt, populated via ingest.py) using local Ollama models to identify root causes.
A remediation agent generates the actual recovery commands; a separate verification agent confirms the fix worked rather than trusting that a command merely ran.
orchestrator.py coordinates the full detect → diagnose → remediate → verify loop across all four agents; the stack runs via docker-compose.
highlights: Root-cause analysis is grounded in a curated incident knowledge base via RAG on Qdrant, not an ungrounded LLM guess.
Diagnosis, remediation, and verification are separate agents with distinct responsibilities rather than one model doing everything.
The verification step is a first-class stage of the loop, not an afterthought — a fix isn't considered done until it's confirmed.

name: GreenML
summary: An AutoML framework that treats power draw as a first-class optimization target alongside accuracy, using real-time CPU/GPU energy measurements to pick model configurations that are actually deployable on low-power and edge hardware.
outcome: balances F1/precision against measured watts, not just FLOPs

detail.problem: Standard AutoML frameworks select models purely on accuracy metrics, which routinely produces winners that are far too power-hungry to run on edge or low-power hardware. GreenML folds real-time energy measurement into the same optimization loop as accuracy, so the model that wins is one that's actually deployable.
architectureNotes: Trains and compares multiple model families (ExtraTrees, RandomForest, k-nearest-neighbors, and a weighted ensemble) via AutoGluon as the underlying AutoML engine.
Wraps model selection with a resource-monitoring layer that records real-time CPU/GPU power draw per training/inference run.
Balances accuracy metrics (F1-score, precision) against measured energy cost rather than optimizing accuracy alone.
highlights: Resource monitoring is integrated directly into the model-selection loop, not bolted on as a post-hoc report.
Model pruning and a preference for lightweight architectures make the winning configuration deployable on low-power and edge devices.
Surfaces an explicit accuracy-vs-energy tradeoff per configuration instead of a single accuracy leaderboard.

name: Ops-Center
summary: A cloud-native incident-response platform — live incident streaming, instant task updates, and role-based collaboration over WebSockets, built to be the single screen a team looks at during a critical event.
outcome: horizontally scalable real-time layer via Redis pub/sub

detail.problem: Incident response for a distributed team usually means a fragmented Slack thread and no single source of truth for who's doing what. Ops-Center is a dedicated war room: live incident state, task tracking, and chat in one role-gated view, updated instantly for everyone watching.
architectureNotes: React + Vite + Tailwind client with dedicated room/chat/action-tracker components and useAuth/useSocket/useRoom hooks over an AuthContext/SocketContext pair.
Node.js + Express server with MongoDB (Mongoose) models for users, rooms, and messages, JWT auth over HTTP-only cookies, and Socket.io for the real-time transport.
Redis pub/sub sits behind Socket.io so events broadcast correctly across multiple server instances — the real-time layer is horizontally scalable from the start, not bolted on for a single process.
highlights: Role-based access control governs who can act during a live incident, not just who can view it.
This is the second, deployed iteration of the concept — an earlier prototype (war-room-devops) proved the real-time architecture before this version was rebuilt and shipped live.

name: Quota Policy Sandbox
summary: Tests whether a proposed resource-allocation policy — API rate limits, compute quotas — holds up fairly before it ships, by training independent reinforcement-learning agents that learn to work the policy rather than following a fixed script.
outcome: isolates what actually drives fair vs. unfair outcomes

detail.problem: Multi-tenant systems that cap a shared resource risk letting a few aggressive tenants dominate usage while others are starved — and testing a proposed cap in production is slow, risky, and sometimes irreversible once real tenants adapt around it. This project stress-tests a policy against agents that genuinely learn how to behave under it, before it's ever deployed for real.
architectureNotes: A shared resource pool that depletes as tenants draw from it and regenerates over time, built as a PettingZoo multi-agent environment.

Each tenant is modeled as an independent agent trained with PPO via Stable-Baselines3 + SuperSuit — no coordination is hardcoded; cooperative or greedy behavior emerges purely from each agent maximizing its own reward.
Population size, overuse penalties, and inter-tenant visibility are varied one at a time, averaged across multiple random seeds, to isolate what actually drives fair vs. unfair outcomes.

A verdict engine translates a proposed policy configuration into a plain-language verdict backed by the measured experimental results; a FastAPI backend serves it to a Next.js frontend where a user configures a policy and compares it against an alternative.
highlights: Fairness or unfairness emerges from what each agent learns to maximize, not from a scripted behavior model.
The verdict is backed by controlled, seeded experiments rather than a single anecdotal run.
